issues.legal_issue: A statutory trust’s proceedings remain valid when the notice fixing the first trustees’ term begins only after their appointment and is delayed until after repeal of the constituting statute.
material_facts: The trustees were appointed under the 1919 Act in 1963, and the trust was incorporated and functioned under that Act.
The notice fixing the commencement of the first trustees’ terms was issued only in 1966, after the Act had been repealed.
The trust had notified the housing scheme in 1965, and the challenge alleged that the late notice meant the trust had never been properly constituted.
The 1919 Act contained a provision validating acts and proceedings despite specified defects or irregularities.
issues.conclusion: The delay in issuing the notice fixing the trustees’ terms did not invalidate the trust’s proceedings, including the framing and implementation of the scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 4 of the U.P. Town Improvement Act, 1919, appointment of the chairman and trustees constituted the trust. Section 8 concerned the duration of their terms, principally to determine when successors should be appointed; it did not make the trust’s competence depend on prompt notice. Section 100 prevented a technical irregularity from invalidating trust proceedings. Sections 96 and 97 of the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1966, addressed repeal and dissolution of the former trusts.

rule.if: statutory_scheme_challenge and trustees_appointed_by_statute and term_start_notice_delayed and validation_provision_covers_irregularities

predicates.statutory_scheme_challenge: The case is a challenge to proceedings taken by a statutory trust in carrying out a scheme.
predicates.trustees_appointed_by_statute: The trust’s chairman and trustees were appointed under the statute that created and incorporated the trust.
predicates.term_start_notice_delayed: The notice fixing the first trustees’ term began was issued after their appointment rather than promptly with it.
predicates.validation_provision_covers_irregulariti: The governing law provides that specified defects or irregularities do not invalidate the trust’s proceedings.

issues.definition: When a statutory scheme challenge concerns trustees appointed under the trust’s creating law, a delayed notice fixing their term does not invalidate proceedings if the governing law protects proceedings from such irregularities.

issues.legal_issue: A scheme commenced under a repealed statute may continue under successor legislation when the scheme’s substantive features have not been shown to have changed.
material_facts: The scheme was first notified under the 1919 Act and was later sanctioned under the 1966 Adhiniyam.

The initial notification was not placed before the Court, and the alleged difference between the scheme descriptions rested on the types of schemes identified in the former Act and a change in the scheme’s Hindi name.
The locality and plots involved were the same in the initial and final notifications.
No substantive alteration to the original scheme was shown.
issues.conclusion: The scheme could continue under the successor legislation because no change beyond its name was shown to prevent its continuation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 97(3) of the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1966, transferred pending schemes and related proceedings under the U.P. Town Improvement Act, 1919, to the successor Board, which could proceed from the stage reached. The party challenging continuation had to show a substantive change that prevented the scheme from continuing; a different name alone did not establish one.

rule.if: successor_law_continuity_challenge and scheme_started_under_repealed_law and same_area_and_plots and no_substantive_change_shown

predicates.successor_law_continuity_challenge: The case challenges whether a scheme begun under a repealed law may continue under successor legislation.
predicates.scheme_started_under_repealed_law: The scheme was initiated under the former law before that law was repealed.
predicates.same_area_and_plots: The initial and later versions of the scheme concern the same locality and plots.
predicates.no_substantive_change_shown: The challenger has not shown a substantive alteration to the scheme beyond a change in its name or description.

issues.definition: A scheme begun under a repealed law may continue under successor legislation when the same area and plots are involved and no substantive change is shown.

issues.legal_issue: Publication of an acquisition declaration after the statutory deadline does not alone invalidate the acquisition when the declaration itself is distinct from its publication and its untimeliness has not been proved.
material_facts: The scheme’s preliminary notice was treated as equivalent to a preliminary notice under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The final notification under the successor enactment was published after the two-year period prescribed by section 4(2) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967.
The record did not establish when the declaration under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was made.
The challenger neither asserted nor proved that the declaration itself was made after the deadline, and did not challenge its existence or bona fides.
issues.conclusion: The late publication of the notification did not invalidate the acquisition because the statutory deadline applied to making the declaration, and no proof showed that the declaration was late.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires the declaration that land is needed for a public purpose; sections 6(2) and 6(3) provide for its publication and its effect as conclusive evidence. Section 4(2) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, imposed the deadline on making the declaration, not on publishing it. The Court relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, [1966] 3 SCR 557, concerning delay in acquisition notifications, while distinguishing a late publication from proof that no timely declaration existed. The challenger bore the burden of proving that the declaration was made late.

rule.if: acquisition_validity_appeal and preliminary_notice_preceded_deadline_period and final_publication_after_deadline and declaration_distinct_from_publication and no_proof_declaration_late

predicates.acquisition_validity_appeal: The case is an appeal challenging the validity of an acquisition for a public scheme.
predicates.preliminary_notice_preceded_deadline_per: The preliminary notice was issued before the period that triggered the statutory deadline for making the declaration.
predicates.final_publication_after_deadline: The notification publishing the declaration appeared after that deadline.
predicates.declaration_distinct_from_publication: The governing procedure treats making the declaration as a separate act from publishing it.
predicates.no_proof_declaration_late: The challenger neither established nor showed that the declaration itself was made after the deadline.

issues.definition: In an acquisition validity appeal, late publication alone does not invalidate the acquisition when making the declaration is distinct from publishing it and the challenger has not shown that the declaration was late.
